title: Advanced Quantum Mechanics
source_note: Graduate-entry-level advanced quantum mechanics topics (perturbation theory, variational method, WKB, angular momentum addition, identical particles, scattering theory, introductory relativistic quantum mechanics) building on PHY301/302, following standard texts such as Griffiths' Introduction to Quantum Mechanics and Sakurai's Modern Quantum Mechanics.

questions.question: In time-independent (Rayleigh-Schrodinger) perturbation theory, the first-order correction to the energy of a non-degenerate state |n> is given by:
options: E_n^(1) = <n|H'|n>, the expectation value of the perturbation in the unperturbed state
E_n^(1) = sum over m of |<m|H'|n>|^2
E_n^(1) = 0 always
questions.correct_answer: E_n^(1) = <n|H'|n>, the expectation value of the perturbation in the unperturbed state
questions.explanation: The first-order energy correction in non-degenerate perturbation theory is simply the expectation value of the perturbing Hamiltonian H' evaluated in the unperturbed eigenstate |n>.

questions.question: In non-degenerate perturbation theory, the first-order correction to the wavefunction |n^(1)> is expressed as an expansion over:
options: Only the state |n> itself
All other unperturbed eigenstates |m> (m ≠ n), weighted by matrix elements <m|H'|n> divided by energy differences
The perturbing potential eigenstates only
A single arbitrary state chosen freely
questions.correct_answer: All other unperturbed eigenstates |m> (m ≠ n), weighted by matrix elements <m|H'|n> divided by energy differences
questions.explanation: The first-order wavefunction correction mixes in contributions from all other unperturbed states, with coefficients <m|H'|n>/(E_n^(0) - E_m^(0)), m ≠ n.

questions.question: Degenerate perturbation theory differs from the non-degenerate case mainly because:
options: One must first diagonalize the perturbation within the degenerate subspace to find the 'good' zeroth-order states before applying standard perturbative formulas
No perturbative correction to energy is possible for degenerate states
The unperturbed Hamiltonian is ignored entirely
Only the second-order energy correction needs to be computed
questions.correct_answer: One must first diagonalize the perturbation within the degenerate subspace to find the 'good' zeroth-order states before applying standard perturbative formulas
questions.explanation: When degeneracy is present, the standard formulas diverge (energy denominators vanish) unless the perturbation is first diagonalized within the degenerate subspace to identify the correct zeroth-order linear combinations.

questions.question: The linear Stark effect (first-order energy shift linear in the applied electric field) is observed in the hydrogen atom's excited states because:
options: Hydrogen's excited states with the same n but different l are degenerate, allowing a non-zero first-order matrix element of the perturbation
Hydrogen has no degenerate states at all
The electric field has no effect on hydrogen
Only the ground state responds to an electric field
questions.correct_answer: Hydrogen's excited states with the same n but different l are degenerate, allowing a non-zero first-order matrix element of the perturbation
questions.explanation: Because states of the same n but different l are degenerate in hydrogen, degenerate perturbation theory applies, and certain matrix elements of the electric dipole perturbation are non-zero, producing a shift linear in the field (unlike most other atoms, which show only a quadratic, second-order Stark effect).

questions.question: Time-dependent perturbation theory is primarily used to calculate:
options: The static energy levels of a time-independent Hamiltonian
Transition probabilities between quantum states induced by a time-varying perturbation
The ground state energy using a trial wavefunction
The classical trajectory of a particle
questions.correct_answer: Transition probabilities between quantum states induced by a time-varying perturbation
questions.explanation: Time-dependent perturbation theory computes the probability amplitude for a system to transition from an initial state to a final state under the influence of a time-dependent perturbing potential.

questions.question: Fermi's golden rule gives the transition rate for a system under a time-dependent perturbation as proportional to:
options: The square of the matrix element of the perturbation between initial and final states, times the density of final states
The perturbation matrix element to the first power only, independent of the density of states
The energy of the initial state alone
The inverse of Planck's constant squared, with no dependence on matrix elements
questions.correct_answer: The square of the matrix element of the perturbation between initial and final states, times the density of final states
questions.explanation: Fermi's golden rule states that the transition rate W = (2*pi/h-bar) * |<f|H'|i>|^2 * rho(E_f), proportional to the squared matrix element and the density of final states rho(E_f).

questions.question: In the interaction of an atom with an oscillating electromagnetic field, the electric dipole approximation assumes that:
options: The wavelength of the radiation is much larger than the size of the atom, so the field is treated as spatially uniform over the atom
The atom has no electric dipole moment
The field varies extremely rapidly within the atomic dimensions
Only magnetic interactions are considered
questions.correct_answer: The wavelength of the radiation is much larger than the size of the atom, so the field is treated as spatially uniform over the atom
questions.explanation: The dipole approximation is valid when the radiation wavelength greatly exceeds atomic dimensions, allowing the spatial variation of the field across the atom to be neglected, simplifying the interaction to an electric dipole coupling.

questions.question: The variational method for estimating the ground state energy of a system relies on the theorem that:
options: The expectation value of the Hamiltonian for any normalized trial wavefunction is always greater than or equal to the true ground state energy
Any trial wavefunction gives exactly the true ground state energy
The expectation value of H for a trial function is always less than the true ground state energy
Trial wavefunctions cannot be used to estimate energies
questions.correct_answer: The expectation value of the Hamiltonian for any normalized trial wavefunction is always greater than or equal to the true ground state energy
questions.explanation: The variational principle guarantees that <psi_trial|H|psi_trial> ≥ E_ground for any normalized trial wavefunction, so minimizing this expectation value over a family of trial functions gives an upper bound estimate of the true ground state energy.

questions.question: When applying the variational method, improving the estimate of the ground state energy is typically achieved by:
options: Using a trial wavefunction with more adjustable (variational) parameters and minimizing the energy expectation value over them
Ignoring the normalization of the trial wavefunction
Choosing a trial function orthogonal to the true ground state
Increasing the mass of the particle in the calculation
questions.correct_answer: Using a trial wavefunction with more adjustable (variational) parameters and minimizing the energy expectation value over them
questions.explanation: A more flexible trial wavefunction (with additional variational parameters) can better approximate the true ground state, and minimizing <H> over these parameters generally yields a lower, more accurate upper-bound energy estimate.

questions.question: The WKB (Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin) approximation is most useful for finding approximate solutions to the Schrodinger equation when:
options: The potential varies slowly (quasi-classically) compared to the particle's de Broglie wavelength
The potential is exactly constant everywhere
The system has no classical analogue at all
The particle is at rest
questions.correct_answer: The potential varies slowly (quasi-classically) compared to the particle's de Broglie wavelength
questions.explanation: The WKB approximation is a semiclassical method valid when the potential changes slowly on the scale of the local de Broglie wavelength, allowing an approximate solution expressed in terms of a classical action integral.

questions.question: The WKB quantization condition for a particle bound in a potential well with two classical turning points is:
options: The integral of the momentum p(x) over one period equals (n + 1/2)*h, for n = 0, 1, 2, ...
The integral of p(x) equals zero always
The energy must equal the potential at the turning points exactly, with no integral condition
p(x) must be constant throughout the well
questions.correct_answer: The integral of the momentum p(x) over one period equals (n + 1/2)*h, for n = 0, 1, 2, ...
questions.explanation: The WKB (Bohr-Sommerfeld) quantization condition states that the closed-path integral of p(x)dx between turning points equals (n+1/2)h, incorporating the Maslov correction from the two turning points.

questions.question: The WKB approximation is commonly applied to estimate the tunnelling probability through a potential barrier by evaluating:
options: An exponential decay factor involving the integral of the imaginary local momentum through the classically forbidden region
The reflection coefficient using only classical mechanics
The barrier height alone, with no integral needed
The particle's rest mass energy
questions.correct_answer: An exponential decay factor involving the integral of the imaginary local momentum through the classically forbidden region
questions.explanation: In WKB tunnelling, the transmission probability is approximately exp(-2*integral of |p(x)|/h-bar dx) evaluated across the classically forbidden region where the kinetic energy is negative.

questions.question: When adding two angular momenta j1 and j2 quantum mechanically, the total angular momentum quantum number j can take values:
options: j = j1 + j2 only
j = j1 * j2
j = 0 only, regardless of j1 and j2
questions.explanation: The rule for combining two angular momenta gives total j ranging in integer steps from |j1 - j2| to j1 + j2, consistent with the triangle inequality.

questions.question: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are used to:
options: Express the coupled total angular momentum eigenstates |j,m> as linear combinations of the uncoupled product states |j1,m1>|j2,m2>
Calculate the energy eigenvalues of the hydrogen atom directly
Determine the spin of a single free electron
Compute the normalization of the wavefunction only
questions.correct_answer: Express the coupled total angular momentum eigenstates |j,m> as linear combinations of the uncoupled product states |j1,m1>|j2,m2>
questions.explanation: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are the expansion coefficients that transform between the uncoupled basis |j1,m1;j2,m2> and the coupled basis |j,m> of total angular momentum.

questions.question: For two spin-1/2 particles, combining their spins gives total spin states with S equal to:
options: S = 0 (singlet) and S = 1 (triplet)
S = 1/2 only
S = 1 only
questions.correct_answer: S = 0 (singlet) and S = 1 (triplet)
questions.explanation: Combining two spin-1/2 particles yields a total spin S = 0 state (the antisymmetric singlet) and S = 1 states (the symmetric triplet, with three m_s values: -1, 0, +1).

questions.question: The Pauli exclusion principle, in its general quantum mechanical form, requires that the total wavefunction of a system of identical fermions be:
options: Symmetric under exchange of any two particles
Antisymmetric under exchange of any two particles
Unchanged in magnitude but arbitrary in phase under particle exchange
Zero everywhere
questions.correct_answer: Antisymmetric under exchange of any two particles
questions.explanation: For identical fermions (half-integer spin particles), the total wavefunction must be antisymmetric under the exchange of any two particles, which is the general statement underlying the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.question: Identical bosons (integer spin particles), unlike fermions, require the total wavefunction to be:
options: Antisymmetric under particle exchange
Symmetric under particle exchange
Always zero when two bosons occupy the same state
Undefined under exchange
questions.correct_answer: Symmetric under particle exchange
questions.explanation: Bosons (integer spin) must have a totally symmetric wavefunction under exchange of any two identical particles, which allows multiple bosons to occupy the same quantum state (unlike fermions).

questions.question: The Slater determinant is a mathematical construction used to:
options: Automatically generate a properly antisymmetrized many-fermion wavefunction from a set of single-particle states
Symmetrize a many-boson wavefunction
Calculate the expectation value of momentum
Solve the free-particle Schrodinger equation in one dimension
questions.correct_answer: Automatically generate a properly antisymmetrized many-fermion wavefunction from a set of single-particle states
questions.explanation: A Slater determinant, formed from single-particle orbitals arranged in a determinant, automatically satisfies antisymmetry under particle exchange, providing a convenient many-fermion wavefunction that respects the Pauli principle.

questions.question: The exchange interaction, an effect with no classical analogue, arises in systems of identical particles due to:
options: The requirement of a (anti)symmetric wavefunction, which introduces an effective interaction-like energy term even without a direct physical force
A newly discovered fundamental force distinct from electromagnetism and gravity
The particles literally exchanging physical positions in space at a finite rate
Relativistic effects only
questions.correct_answer: The requirement of a (anti)symmetric wavefunction, which introduces an effective interaction-like energy term even without a direct physical force
questions.explanation: Exchange effects arise purely from the symmetrization postulate applied to identical particles' wavefunctions; they alter expectation values of energy (e.g., in helium or ferromagnetism) without being a distinct physical force.

questions.question: In quantum scattering theory, the differential cross-section dsigma/dOmega is related to the scattering amplitude f(theta) by:
options: dsigma/dOmega = |f(theta)|^2
dsigma/dOmega = f(theta)
dsigma/dOmega = 1/f(theta)
dsigma/dOmega = f(theta)^3
questions.correct_answer: dsigma/dOmega = |f(theta)|^2
questions.explanation: The differential scattering cross-section is given by the modulus squared of the scattering amplitude, dsigma/dOmega = |f(theta)|^2, analogous to how probability relates to a wavefunction's modulus squared.

questions.question: The first Born approximation in scattering theory assumes that:
options: The scattering potential is weak enough that the incident wave is only slightly perturbed, allowing the scattered wave to be computed using the unperturbed incident wave inside the interaction integral
The potential is infinitely strong
The particle has zero incident energy
Scattering occurs only at exactly 180 degrees
questions.correct_answer: The scattering potential is weak enough that the incident wave is only slightly perturbed, allowing the scattered wave to be computed using the unperturbed incident wave inside the interaction integral
questions.explanation: The Born approximation treats the scattering potential perturbatively, replacing the exact wavefunction inside the integral for the scattering amplitude with the unperturbed incident plane wave, valid for weak potentials or high energy.

questions.question: In the Born approximation, the scattering amplitude f(theta) is essentially the Fourier transform of:
options: The scattering potential V(r)
The incident particle's kinetic energy
The total cross-section only
The particle's spin state
questions.correct_answer: The scattering potential V(r)
questions.explanation: In the first Born approximation, the scattering amplitude is proportional to the three-dimensional Fourier transform of the scattering potential V(r) with respect to the momentum transfer vector.

questions.question: The partial wave analysis method for scattering decomposes the incident and scattered waves into components of definite:
options: Orbital angular momentum l
Spin only
Electric charge
Rest mass
questions.correct_answer: Orbital angular momentum l
questions.explanation: Partial wave analysis expands the scattering wavefunction in terms of Legendre polynomials corresponding to definite orbital angular momentum quantum numbers l, useful particularly for low-energy, spherically symmetric potential scattering.

questions.question: In partial wave analysis, the phase shift delta_l for each partial wave characterizes:
options: The change in phase of the l-th partial wave caused by the scattering potential, relative to the free-particle wave
The total energy of the incident particle
The mass of the target particle
The exact position of the scattered particle
questions.correct_answer: The change in phase of the l-th partial wave caused by the scattering potential, relative to the free-particle wave
questions.explanation: The phase shift delta_l quantifies how much the scattering potential shifts the phase of the asymptotic radial wavefunction for angular momentum l compared to the free-particle case, and the full set of phase shifts determines the scattering amplitude and cross-section.

questions.question: The optical theorem in scattering theory relates the total scattering cross-section to:
options: The imaginary part of the forward (theta = 0) scattering amplitude
The real part of the backward scattering amplitude
The particle's rest mass only
The scattering angle theta = 90 degrees exclusively
questions.correct_answer: The imaginary part of the forward (theta = 0) scattering amplitude
questions.explanation: The optical theorem states that the total cross-section sigma_total is proportional to the imaginary part of the forward scattering amplitude f(0), reflecting conservation of probability (unitarity) in the scattering process.

questions.question: The Klein-Gordon equation is a relativistic wave equation that describes:
options: Spin-1/2 particles exclusively
Spin-0 (scalar) particles, obtained by relativistically quantizing the energy-momentum relation E^2 = p^2*c^2 + m^2*c^4
Only massless particles
Classical, non-quantum fields exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Spin-0 (scalar) particles, obtained by relativistically quantizing the energy-momentum relation E^2 = p^2*c^2 + m^2*c^4
questions.explanation: The Klein-Gordon equation is the relativistic wave equation for spin-0 particles, derived by applying the quantum operator substitutions to the relativistic energy-momentum relation E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4.

questions.question: A key historical problem with the Klein-Gordon equation, when first interpreted as a single-particle wave equation, was that:
options: It gave rise to a probability density that could become negative, so it could not be interpreted the same way as the Schrodinger probability density
It could not describe any particle with nonzero mass
It violated Newton's laws of motion
It had no solutions at all
questions.correct_answer: It gave rise to a probability density that could become negative, so it could not be interpreted the same way as the Schrodinger probability density
questions.explanation: Because the Klein-Gordon equation is second-order in time, its associated conserved current can have a density that is not positive-definite, undermining a direct single-particle probability interpretation (later resolved by reinterpreting it as a field equation).

questions.question: The Dirac equation was formulated to describe relativistic spin-1/2 particles and, unlike the Klein-Gordon equation, is:
options: Second order in time derivatives, just like Klein-Gordon
First order in both space and time derivatives, and naturally incorporates electron spin
Applicable only to spin-0 particles
A purely classical (non-quantum) equation
questions.correct_answer: First order in both space and time derivatives, and naturally incorporates electron spin
questions.explanation: The Dirac equation is linear (first order) in both time and spatial derivatives, and its four-component spinor solutions naturally include electron spin as well as predicting the existence of antiparticles.

questions.question: One of the notable theoretical predictions of the Dirac equation, later confirmed experimentally, was:
options: The existence of antiparticles (such as the positron)
The exact value of the fine structure constant
The non-existence of electron spin
That all particles must be massless
questions.correct_answer: The existence of antiparticles (such as the positron)
questions.explanation: The Dirac equation's negative-energy solutions led Dirac to predict the existence of a positively charged counterpart to the electron, the positron, which was subsequently discovered experimentally by Anderson in 1932.

questions.question: Second quantization (the formalism of creation and annihilation operators) is particularly useful for describing:
options: Single, isolated particles with no interactions
Many-particle systems where the number of particles can change, and for handling identical particle statistics systematically
Purely classical fields with no quantum behaviour
Only systems with exactly one fermion and one boson
questions.correct_answer: Many-particle systems where the number of particles can change, and for handling identical particle statistics systematically
questions.explanation: Second quantization uses creation and annihilation operators acting on Fock space to elegantly describe systems with variable particle number, automatically encoding the correct (anti)symmetrization for bosons and fermions.

questions.question: For bosonic creation and annihilation operators a-dagger and a, the fundamental commutation relation is:
options: [a, a-dagger] = 1
{a, a-dagger} = 1 (anticommutator)
[a, a-dagger] = 0
a*a-dagger = 0
questions.correct_answer: [a, a-dagger] = 1
questions.explanation: Bosonic ladder operators satisfy the commutation relation [a, a-dagger] = a*a-dagger - a-dagger*a = 1, which underlies the quantization of the harmonic oscillator and bosonic field theories.

questions.question: For fermionic creation and annihilation operators, the Pauli exclusion principle is naturally encoded through:
options: Commutation relations identical to those of bosons
Anticommutation relations, such that applying the same creation operator twice gives zero
The requirement that all fermion operators commute with the Hamiltonian
There being no algebraic relation at all between fermionic operators
questions.correct_answer: Anticommutation relations, such that applying the same creation operator twice gives zero
questions.explanation: Fermionic operators satisfy anticommutation relations {a_i, a_j-dagger} = delta_ij, which implies (a-dagger)^2 = 0, automatically preventing two fermions from occupying the same quantum state, consistent with the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.question: The Zeeman effect on an atom placed in a weak external magnetic field is treated, in advanced quantum mechanics, as an example of:
options: A time-dependent perturbation with no analytical solution
A perturbation to the atomic Hamiltonian via degenerate (or near-degenerate) perturbation theory, splitting the otherwise degenerate m_j sublevels
A purely classical phenomenon unrelated to quantum perturbation theory
The WKB approximation applied to a free particle
questions.correct_answer: A perturbation to the atomic Hamiltonian via degenerate (or near-degenerate) perturbation theory, splitting the otherwise degenerate m_j sublevels
questions.explanation: The weak-field Zeeman effect is analysed using perturbation theory, treating the interaction of the atom's magnetic moment with the external field as a perturbation that lifts the degeneracy among different m_j sublevels within a given J level.

questions.question: The helium atom's ground state energy cannot be found exactly analytically because:
options: It is a three-body problem (two electrons and the nucleus) with an electron-electron repulsion term that makes the Schrodinger equation non-separable
Helium has no ground state
The Schrodinger equation does not apply to multi-electron atoms
Helium's nucleus has no charge
questions.correct_answer: It is a three-body problem (two electrons and the nucleus) with an electron-electron repulsion term that makes the Schrodinger equation non-separable
questions.explanation: The electron-electron Coulomb repulsion term in helium's Hamiltonian prevents exact separation of variables, so approximate methods (perturbation theory, the variational method) are needed to estimate its ground state energy.
